screens.title: Polymorphism and Virtual Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we'll open a central toolbox of object-oriented design in C++: polymorphism and virtual functions. Polymorphism lets objects from different classes behave under a common interface so your code can work with a family of types without knowing their concrete forms. You will learn how compile-time mechanisms like function overloading differ from runtime polymorphism achieved with virtual functions, and why the virtual table and a hidden object pointer are key to this behavior. We'll step through a classic Shape example that uses base class pointers and smart pointers to call derived draw methods, and we'll inspect how pure virtual functions let you define abstract interfaces. Along the way you will see common pitfalls: object slicing when passing by value and the serious bug of non-virtual destructors that can cause resource leaks. By the end you will understand how to design class hierarchies that are flexible, maintainable, and safe. Think about a GUI toolkit where every widget responds to handleEvent differently — polymorphism makes that design possible. Ready to explore the mechanisms and the patterns that make it robust?

Second, you'll implement runtime polymorphism by declaring virtual functions and using pointers or references to base types; you'll see how calling a method through a base pointer triggers the derived implementation at runtime. screens.title: What is Polymorphism in C++?
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism literally means many forms: a single interface presenting different behaviors depending on the concrete object. In C++ this idea appears in two broad categories. Compile-time polymorphism is when the compiler decides which function to call, for example with overloading or operator overloads. Runtime polymorphism happens when a base class declares a function as virtual and derived classes override that function. The program then defers the decision of which implementation to invoke until it knows the actual type at runtime. Why is that important? It decouples client code from concrete implementations. For instance, a rendering loop that operates on a list of shapes can call draw on each base pointer and trust that each derived shape draws itself correctly without special casing. A common misconception is that polymorphism is only about inheritance; it is about substitutability — a derived object should be usable wherever a base is expected. A practical caution: only pointers or references preserve polymorphic identity. Passing derived objects by value to a function that takes a base parameter causes object slicing, where derived parts are lost. Takeaway: when you need interchangeable behaviors that can grow over time, design with runtime polymorphism using virtual functions and base pointers. How might that change the way you structure your class responsibilities?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Polymorphism lets code treat different concrete types through a common interface, enabling interchangeable behaviors and extensible designs.

content.html:
Core Concept
What is Polymorphism?
A single interface used by many concrete types.
Quick definition

Polymorphism allows objects of different derived classes to respond differently to the same function call through a shared base type.

Analogy

Think of an electrical outlet: many devices plug in and each behaves according to its design though the plug interface is the same.

Example
A renderer loops over Shape pointers and calls draw(); each concrete shape provides its own implementation so the renderer remains unchanged when new shapes are added.
Key Takeaway

Use polymorphism to separate what code does from how specific types implement the behavior.

Definition Visual
Compile-time
Overloading and templates where the compiler selects the function.
Runtime
Virtual functions, vtable lookups, and dynamic dispatch using base pointers or references.
Misconception
Polymorphism is not automatically present with inheritance; methods must be virtual and objects must be accessed via pointers or references to enable runtime behavior.

screens.title: Compile-time vs Runtime Polymorphism
screens.narratorSegment: Let's compare the two major flavors of polymorphism so you can choose the right tool. Compile-time polymorphism includes function overloading and operator overloading; the compiler resolves the exact function based on argument types and count. It's fast because no runtime lookup is needed, and it's useful for function families that are conceptually the same but accept different parameter types. Runtime polymorphism, in contrast, uses virtual functions: the compiler generates a vtable for classes with virtual functions and objects store a pointer to that table. At runtime, calling a virtual method through a base pointer consults the vtable to resolve the actual implementation. This allows extensibility: new derived classes can be added without touching the calling code. A practical example: overloading is appropriate for formatting functions with different parameter lists, while virtual functions are appropriate when different derived objects must implement a behavior like draw or handleEvent. A common trade-off is performance and flexibility: virtual dispatch has a small runtime cost for lookup but gains in extensibility. Be careful not to confuse the two: simply overloading does not provide runtime substitution. In your designs, prefer compile-time choices when behavior is static and known, and use runtime polymorphism when behavior must vary with object identity.

keyIdea.title: Comparison summary
keyIdea.text: Compile-time uses signature resolution by the compiler; runtime uses vtable lookups and base pointers to defer decisions to execution time.

content.html:
Comparison
Compile-time vs Runtime
Compile-time Polymorphism
  • Resolved by the compiler using function signatures.
  • Examples: function overloading, operator overloading, templates.
  • Fast, but not substitutable at runtime.
Runtime Polymorphism
  • Enabled by declaring functions virtual in a base class.
  • Uses vtable and vptr to select the implementation at runtime.
  • Supports extensibility: add derived types without changing client code.
Practical rule
Use compile-time polymorphism when parameter choices vary; use runtime polymorphism when implementation depends on object type.
Concrete Example
Suppose you have multiple print functions that accept different formats. Overloading chooses the right one at compile time. If instead you have a base Logger with derived FileLogger and ConsoleLogger, declaring log as virtual lets code call log through a Logger pointer and let the derived logger handle the message at runtime.
Misconception check
Overloading a method of the base class does not make that call polymorphic when invoked through a base pointer. The base function must be virtual for dynamic dispatch to occur.
Key Takeaway

Choose the form of polymorphism based on whether you need runtime substitution or compile-time selection.

screens.title: Enabling Runtime Polymorphism
screens.narratorSegment: There is a small checklist to make runtime polymorphism work reliably. Step one: declare the base class function as virtual. This tells the compiler to create per-class vtables. Step two: in the derived class provide an overriding implementation, and prefer the override keyword to let the compiler check your intent. Step three: use pointers or references to the base type when you store or pass objects. This preserves polymorphic identity and ensures dynamic dispatch will check the object's vptr at runtime. Step four: always make the base class destructor virtual when you intend to delete derived objects through base pointers; otherwise derived destructors won't run and resources can leak. A common error is passing by value — this slices derived content into a base copy, and virtual calls then operate on the sliced object. Another subtle point: you can still call a virtual function directly on a concrete object variable; the dynamic lookup matters only when calling through a pointer or reference. Example sequence: declare virtual void draw() const in Shape, override draw in Circle and Square and put std::unique_ptr into a vector. Iterating and calling draw will dispatch correctly to Circle or Square. Use the override specifier and smart pointers to combine safety and clarity.

keyIdea.title: Process to enable
keyIdea.text: Virtual declaration, override in derived, store via pointers/references, and use virtual destructors for safe cleanup.

content.html:
Process Flow
Steps to Enable Runtime Polymorphism
1.
Declare virtual in base
Mark the function virtual to trigger vtable generation.
2.
Override in derived
Provide derived implementations and use override to catch mistakes.
3.
Use pointers or references
Store objects polymorphically in pointers or references, not by value.
4.
Virtual destructor
Ensure proper cleanup when deleting through a base pointer.
Misconception: Declaring derived methods with the same name is not enough; the base must be virtual for dynamic dispatch through base pointers.
Concrete Checklist
Code pattern
virtual void draw() const; // base class Circle : public Shape { void draw() const override; } // derived
Pro tip
Prefer override to catch signature mismatches and use smart pointers like unique_ptr to manage lifetimes.
Common mistake
Passing by value causes slicing and defeats polymorphism. Use references or pointers instead.

screens.title: vtable, vptr, and Dynamic Dispatch
screens.narratorSegment: To reason about runtime behavior you should understand the vtable mechanism. When a class declares at least one virtual function, the compiler builds a table for that class that contains pointers to the virtual functions' implementations — this is the vtable. Each object of that class contains a hidden pointer, commonly called vptr, which points to the class's vtable. When you call a virtual function through a base pointer or reference, the program uses the vptr to find the vtable and then calls the function address stored there. This lookup is the essence of dynamic dispatch. One useful mental model is: the vtable is a per-class dispatch table and the vptr is per-object glue linking the object to its class's behavior. A common misconception is that vtables are language-level artifacts you write; they are generated by the compiler. The important practical effects are that virtual calls are slightly more expensive due to an indirection, and that polymorphism works even when the exact derived type wasn't known at compile time. Also remember that pure virtual functions appear in the table to enforce derived overrides, and the destructor ordering still follows derived then base when destructors are virtual. Understanding this lets you balance design and performance in contexts like inner loops or performance-sensitive systems.

keyIdea.title: Mechanics
keyIdea.text: The vtable holds addresses of virtual functions and the object's vptr points to its class's vtable so calls through base pointers dispatch correctly at runtime.

content.html:
Mechanism
vtable and vptr
A per-class table of function addresses and a per-object pointer that links to it.
vtable
A compiler-generated table holding pointers to the virtual implementations for a class.
vptr
A hidden pointer in each object that points to that object's class vtable.
Dynamic dispatch
A call through a base pointer uses the object's vptr to find and call the correct function address at runtime.
Annotated View
Class A vtable
[ <addr> draw, <addr> print, <addr> ~A ]
Object instance layout
vptr → points to Class A vtable; data members follow vptr in memory layout.
Why it matters
Understanding vtables helps explain why virtual calls have one indirection and why destructors must be virtual for correct cleanup order.

screens.title: Shape Hierarchy Live Coding
screens.narratorSegment: Now we'll walk through a compact, practical example that puts the earlier concepts into code. The base Shape class declares virtual void draw() const and a virtual destructor. Circle and Square override draw. In main, a std::vector of std::unique_ptr stores instances created with make_unique for Circle, Square, and even Shape itself. Iterating over the vector and calling shape_ptr->draw() invokes the correct derived draw because the call is virtual and the unique_ptr preserves a base pointer to a derived object. This demonstrates three important ideas: use of virtual methods, the safety of smart pointers for ownership, and how runtime dispatch enables a single loop to handle different behaviors. A common error students make is creating objects by value in the vector; that slices derived parts. Another subtlety: putting a base class object into the same collection is allowed but it will call the base implementation for that element. Finally, when deleting a derived object via a base pointer, a virtual destructor ensures the derived destructor runs first, avoiding resource leaks. Try extending the example by adding a new shape — the loop needs no changes. That is the power of polymorphism.

keyIdea.title: Live coding insight
keyIdea.text: Using unique_ptr<Shape> in a vector demonstrates safe ownership and correct runtime dispatch when calling virtual methods.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Shape example
Read the code to see how virtual draw and smart pointers work together.
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <memory>

class Shape {
public:
  virtual void draw() const { std::cout << "Drawing a generic shape." << std::endl; }
  virtual ~Shape() { std::cout << "Shape destructor called." << std::endl; }
};

class Circle : public Shape {
public:
  void draw() const override { std::cout << "Drawing a Circle." << std::endl; }
  ~Circle() { std::cout << "Circle destructor called." << std::endl; }
};

int main() {
  std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Shape>> shapes;
  shapes.push_back(std::make_unique<Circle>());
  shapes.push_back(std::make_unique<Shape>());

  for (const auto & s : shapes) {
    s->draw(); // dynamic dispatch
  }
}
Output will include Drawing a Circle. and Drawing a generic shape., and destructors called when unique_ptr releases objects. Try adding a Square derived class; no changes to the loop are needed.
Explanation
  • unique_ptr preserves polymorphic ownership and prevents leaks.
  • virtual draw and override ensure correct method selection at runtime.
  • Putting a base object into the vector is allowed; its draw remains the base implementation.
Try this
Replace the base object entry with a Square derived class and observe the draw calls change automatically.

screens.title: Virtual Destructors: Cleanup and Safety
screens.narratorSegment: This screen focuses on the destructor rule, a safety-critical detail. If a base class with virtual functions has a non-virtual destructor, deleting a derived object through a base pointer calls only the base destructor. The derived class's destructor — where derived-only resources would be released — is skipped, producing leaks or undefined behavior. The correct pattern is to declare the base destructor virtual. Doing so ensures the destructor call chain runs from derived to base, releasing derived resources first. The chapter provides a concrete FileLogger example where the derived class allocates a buffer; with a non-virtual base destructor the buffer leaks. In practice, always mark the destructor virtual in polymorphic base classes, even if the body is defaulted. When combined with smart pointers like unique_ptr, virtual destructors ensure predictable destruction order. A common misconception is that virtual destructors are only for rare cases — in polymorphic hierarchies they are essential. If the base class is intended purely as an interface with no state, prefer virtual defaulted destructors to guarantee safety without additional code. The final question to hold in mind: what could happen in a long-running system if cleanup is skipped?

keyIdea.title: Safety rule
keyIdea.text: Declare base destructors virtual in any class meant to be used polymorphically to ensure derived destructors execute and resources are freed.

content.html:
Live Demo
Virtual destructor example
Compare non-virtual and virtual base destructor behaviors.
// Non-virtual base destructor: dangerous
class Logger {
public:
  ~Logger() { std::cout << "Logger destructor called." << std::endl; }
};

class FileLogger : public Logger {
  char* buf = new char[100];
public:
  ~FileLogger() { delete[] buf; std::cout << "FileLogger destructor called." << std::endl; }
};

// delete base_ptr when base destructor not virtual => FileLogger destructor skipped

// Correct pattern:
class LoggerSafe {
public:
  virtual ~LoggerSafe() { std::cout << "LoggerSafe destructor" << std::endl; }
};
With a virtual destructor both derived and base destructors run in proper order. Without it, cleanup in the derived destructor is skipped and resources leak. This is not theoretical — it affects long-running programs and code that manages file handles, network sockets, or heap memory in derived classes.
Checklist
  • Mark base destructors virtual in polymorphic classes.
  • Prefer virtual default destructor if no custom cleanup is needed.
  • Combine with smart pointers to manage ownership safely.
Key Takeaway
Virtual destructors ensure derived cleanup runs when deleting through a base pointer.

screens.title: Pure Virtual Functions and Abstract Classes
screens.narratorSegment: Pure virtual functions are the language tool for expressing an abstract operation without providing a base implementation. You write a pure virtual function by appending equals zero to its declaration, for example declare virtual void draw() const = 0; in a Drawable base. Any class with one or more pure virtual functions becomes abstract and cannot be instantiated. Its purpose is to define a contract: derived classes must implement the pure virtual functions or themselves remain abstract. This pattern is the closest C++ has to an interface: a class with only pure virtual functions and a virtual destructor effectively defines a behavior contract that all implementers must follow. Concrete benefit: the compiler enforces that derived types implement required methods, preventing omissions at runtime. A misconception is that pure virtual functions must never have an implementation; in fact you can provide a base implementation while still making the function pure virtual, but that's an advanced use for shared functionality. The typical use is to keep the base lean and force derived types to supply the behavior. When designing systems, use abstract classes to capture the responsibilities you expect every implementer to have, then write code that depends only on that contract.

keyIdea.title: Abstract interface
keyIdea.text: Pure virtual functions make a class abstract and define an interface that derived classes must implement.

content.html:
Definition
Pure Virtual & Abstract Class
A pure virtual function sets a required contract for derived classes and makes the base abstract.
Key points
  • Declare with = 0 to make a function pure virtual.
  • An abstract class cannot be instantiated directly.
  • Use virtual destructor with abstract bases to ensure safe cleanup.
Example Interface
class Drawable {
public:
  virtual void draw() const = 0; // pure virtual
  virtual ~Drawable() = default;  // virtual destructor
};
Any class inheriting Drawable must provide draw to become concrete. This pattern enforces consistent behavior across implementers.

screens.title: Command Processor: Hands-on Task
screens.narratorSegment: This activity applies abstract classes and runtime polymorphism to a small, practical design: a Command Processor. The plan is simple and maps directly to the chapter's template. First, create an abstract base class Command with a pure virtual execute() and a virtual destructor. Second, derive concrete commands like PrintCommand, SaveCommand, and ExitCommand and override execute to perform their action. Third, in main create a std::vector of std::unique_ptr, push back each concrete command using make_unique, then iterate and call execute on each command pointer. This demonstrates polymorphism: the vector holds base pointers to different concrete types, and each execute runs the appropriate implementation. While implementing, watch for two mistakes: do not store commands by value in the vector and ensure the base destructor is virtual so destructors run correctly when unique_ptr releases objects. This exercise also highlights programming to an interface: client code treats every command as a Command and is agnostic to how each one is implemented. After completing the template, try adding a new command type without changing the processor logic to see the design's extensibility. Hands-on Activity
Command Processor
Follow the template to implement a polymorphic command processor.
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>
#include <memory>

class Command {
public:
  virtual void execute() = 0; // pure virtual
  virtual ~Command() { std::cout << "Command destructor called." << std::endl; }
};

// Implement PrintCommand, SaveCommand, ExitCommand each overriding execute()
// In main create std::vector<std::unique_ptr<Command>> and push_back instances, then iterate and call execute().
Scaffolding & Tips
  • Use make_unique to construct commands into the vector.
  • Keep execute parameterless for simplicity in this exercise.
  • Verify destructors print messages to confirm proper destruction order.
Challenge
Add a new command type and ensure the processor executes it without any changes to the processing loop.

screens.title: Object Slicing: What Goes Wrong
screens.narratorSegment: Object slicing is an easy mistake with surprising consequences. It happens when a derived object is copied into a base class object by value. Because the base object has no storage for derived-only members, those members are dropped during the copy. The result is that the copied object becomes a plain base object and any virtual calls on that copy will dispatch to the base implementation. A typical scenario: you write a function that takes Base by value and pass a Derived instance. The derived parts are sliced away, and you no longer have polymorphism. To avoid slicing, pass objects by pointer or reference, or use smart pointers for ownership. Another subtle place slicing shows up is when you store objects by value in containers typed to the base class. Instead, store pointers to preserve the dynamic type. A misconception is thinking slicing only affects data; it also affects behavior because the runtime type is lost and virtual dispatch no longer reaches derived implementations. The correct practice is to treat polymorphic types as non-copyable by value or only copy through explicit clone methods that preserve dynamic type, but the simplest rule for now is: do not pass polymorphic objects by value.

keyIdea.title: Slicing rule
keyIdea.text: Avoid copying derived objects into base class variables; pass by pointer/reference or use pointers in containers to preserve derived parts and behavior.

content.html:
Common Pitfall
Object Slicing
Slicing removes derived-specific data and behavior when copying by value to a base object.
Bad example
Derived d; Base b = d; // slices derived parts
Avoidance
  • Pass by reference or pointer instead of by value.
  • Store pointers (smart pointers) in containers instead of object slices.
  • Use clone methods if you need to copy polymorphically.
Concrete remedy
Change functions that take Base b to take const Base& b or Base* b. Using const references avoids copies and preserves the derived object identity so virtual functions continue to dispatch to derived implementations.
Misconception
Slicing is not just a missing field; methods that depend on derived behavior will also break because the dynamic type is lost.

screens.title: Design Patterns and Practical Advice
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism is a design enabler, but effective use requires consistent patterns. First, program to an interface: depend on abstract classes with pure virtual functions rather than concrete implementations. This reduces coupling and makes adding new types straightforward. Second, prefer smart pointers like std::unique_ptr when managing polymorphic objects to avoid manual delete and to ensure RAII semantics. Third, always declare base destructors virtual for polymorphic hierarchies. Fourth, use override to make intent explicit and let the compiler help you. Fifth, avoid storing polymorphic objects by value to prevent slicing. Sixth, document ownership: whether a function expects to take ownership (unique_ptr) or temporary access (raw pointer or reference). Finally, test destructor behavior by instrumenting destructors in examples; confirm derived destructors run when deleting through base pointers. These practices make polymorphic code safer, clearer, and maintainable. One last tip: when performance is critical and virtual call overhead matters, measure and consider alternatives like function objects or templates where appropriate, but remember you trade extensibility for those gains. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical rules
keyIdea.text: Program to interfaces, use smart pointers, make destructors virtual, and avoid slicing to build maintainable polymorphic systems.

content.html:
Best Practices
Design and Safety
Program to interfaces: depend on abstract base classes or pure virtual interfaces.
Use smart pointers: unique_ptr enforces ownership and prevents leaks.
Mark destructors virtual: essential for polymorphic cleanup.
Declare override: catches accidental signature mismatches.
Practical checklist
  • Do not pass polymorphic objects by value.
  • Store polymorphic objects via pointers in containers.
  • Document ownership and lifetime expectations for functions that accept pointers.
  • Measure virtual call overhead only when necessary and prefer templates for static polymorphism if performance demands.
Key Takeaway

Follow these patterns to keep polymorphic code robust, extensible, and safe.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson we'll open a central toolbox of object-oriented design in C++: polymorphism and virtual functions. Polymorphism lets objects from different classes behave under a common interface so your code can work with a family of types without knowing their concrete forms. You will learn how compile-time mechanisms like function overloading differ from runtime polymorphism achieved with virtual functions, and why the virtual table and a hidden object pointer are key to this behavior. We'll step through a classic Shape example that uses base class pointers and smart pointers to call derived draw methods, and we'll inspect how pure virtual functions let you define abstract interfaces. Along the way you will see common pitfalls: object slicing when passing by value and the serious bug of non-virtual destructors that can cause resource leaks. By the end you will understand how to design class hierarchies that are flexible, maintainable, and safe. Think about a GUI toolkit where every widget responds to handleEvent differently — polymorphism makes that design possible. Ready to explore the mechanisms and the patterns that make it robust?

These objectives lay out concrete abilities you will gain. First, you will explain polymorphism and clearly tell apart compile-time mechanisms like overloading from runtime behavior driven by virtual functions. That matters because choosing static or dynamic dispatch affects extensibility and performance. Second, you'll implement runtime polymorphism by declaring virtual functions and using pointers or references to base types; you'll see how calling a method through a base pointer triggers the derived implementation at runtime. Third, you'll understand pure virtual functions and abstract classes so you can define interfaces that force derived types to implement required operations. Lastly on this first page, you will identify common pitfalls such as object slicing and the hazard of non-virtual destructors. Each objective will be paired with a small mnemonic or scenario to make it easier to recall. These are practical skills: writing a Shape collection or a Command processor relies on these techniques. As you practice, check the verified competency milestone to ensure you can both reason about and implement these patterns correctly.

On this page we'll translate goals into tasks you can apply at the keyboard. You will learn to apply polymorphic principles when designing class hierarchies, so code becomes easier to extend with new types without changing client code. You'll practice programming to an interface: rely on pure virtual contracts rather than concrete classes. You'll also inspect the virtual table mechanism so you can reason about runtime behavior and performance implications. Finally, you'll complete a hands-on Command Processor task that assembles a vector of command objects and executes them through base pointers, showing how polymorphism simplifies processing a family of actions. These objectives are focused on real code: you'll build and run examples, spot a slicing bug, and check destructor behavior to ensure correct cleanup. Successful completion means you can both explain why virtual is needed and implement it safely in designs that scale.

Polymorphism literally means many forms: a single interface presenting different behaviors depending on the concrete object. In C++ this idea appears in two broad categories. Compile-time polymorphism is when the compiler decides which function to call, for example with overloading or operator overloads. Runtime polymorphism happens when a base class declares a function as virtual and derived classes override that function. The program then defers the decision of which implementation to invoke until it knows the actual type at runtime. Why is that important? It decouples client code from concrete implementations. For instance, a rendering loop that operates on a list of shapes can call draw on each base pointer and trust that each derived shape draws itself correctly without special casing. A common misconception is that polymorphism is only about inheritance; it is about substitutability — a derived object should be usable wherever a base is expected. A practical caution: only pointers or references preserve polymorphic identity. Passing derived objects by value to a function that takes a base parameter causes object slicing, where derived parts are lost. Takeaway: when you need interchangeable behaviors that can grow over time, design with runtime polymorphism using virtual functions and base pointers. How might that change the way you structure your class responsibilities?

Let's compare the two major flavors of polymorphism so you can choose the right tool. Compile-time polymorphism includes function overloading and operator overloading; the compiler resolves the exact function based on argument types and count. It's fast because no runtime lookup is needed, and it's useful for function families that are conceptually the same but accept different parameter types. Runtime polymorphism, in contrast, uses virtual functions: the compiler generates a vtable for classes with virtual functions and objects store a pointer to that table. At runtime, calling a virtual method through a base pointer consults the vtable to resolve the actual implementation. This allows extensibility: new derived classes can be added without touching the calling code. A practical example: overloading is appropriate for formatting functions with different parameter lists, while virtual functions are appropriate when different derived objects must implement a behavior like draw or handleEvent. A common trade-off is performance and flexibility: virtual dispatch has a small runtime cost for lookup but gains in extensibility. Be careful not to confuse the two: simply overloading does not provide runtime substitution. In your designs, prefer compile-time choices when behavior is static and known, and use runtime polymorphism when behavior must vary with object identity.

There is a small checklist to make runtime polymorphism work reliably. Step one: declare the base class function as virtual. This tells the compiler to create per-class vtables. Step two: in the derived class provide an overriding implementation, and prefer the override keyword to let the compiler check your intent. Step three: use pointers or references to the base type when you store or pass objects. This preserves polymorphic identity and ensures dynamic dispatch will check the object's vptr at runtime. Step four: always make the base class destructor virtual when you intend to delete derived objects through base pointers; otherwise derived destructors won't run and resources can leak. A common error is passing by value — this slices derived content into a base copy, and virtual calls then operate on the sliced object. Another subtle point: you can still call a virtual function directly on a concrete object variable; the dynamic lookup matters only when calling through a pointer or reference. Example sequence: declare virtual void draw() const in Shape, override draw in Circle and Square and put std::unique_ptr into a vector. Iterating and calling draw will dispatch correctly to Circle or Square. Use the override specifier and smart pointers to combine safety and clarity.

To reason about runtime behavior you should understand the vtable mechanism. When a class declares at least one virtual function, the compiler builds a table for that class that contains pointers to the virtual functions' implementations — this is the vtable. Each object of that class contains a hidden pointer, commonly called vptr, which points to the class's vtable. When you call a virtual function through a base pointer or reference, the program uses the vptr to find the vtable and then calls the function address stored there. This lookup is the essence of dynamic dispatch. One useful mental model is: the vtable is a per-class dispatch table and the vptr is per-object glue linking the object to its class's behavior. A common misconception is that vtables are language-level artifacts you write; they are generated by the compiler. The important practical effects are that virtual calls are slightly more expensive due to an indirection, and that polymorphism works even when the exact derived type wasn't known at compile time. Also remember that pure virtual functions appear in the table to enforce derived overrides, and the destructor ordering still follows derived then base when destructors are virtual. Understanding this lets you balance design and performance in contexts like inner loops or performance-sensitive systems.

Now we'll walk through a compact, practical example that puts the earlier concepts into code. The base Shape class declares virtual void draw() const and a virtual destructor. Circle and Square override draw. In main, a std::vector of std::unique_ptr stores instances created with make_unique for Circle, Square, and even Shape itself. Iterating over the vector and calling shape_ptr->draw() invokes the correct derived draw because the call is virtual and the unique_ptr preserves a base pointer to a derived object. This demonstrates three important ideas: use of virtual methods, the safety of smart pointers for ownership, and how runtime dispatch enables a single loop to handle different behaviors. A common error students make is creating objects by value in the vector; that slices derived parts. Another subtlety: putting a base class object into the same collection is allowed but it will call the base implementation for that element. Finally, when deleting a derived object via a base pointer, a virtual destructor ensures the derived destructor runs first, avoiding resource leaks. Try extending the example by adding a new shape — the loop needs no changes. That is the power of polymorphism.

This screen focuses on the destructor rule, a safety-critical detail. If a base class with virtual functions has a non-virtual destructor, deleting a derived object through a base pointer calls only the base destructor. The derived class's destructor — where derived-only resources would be released — is skipped, producing leaks or undefined behavior. The correct pattern is to declare the base destructor virtual. Doing so ensures the destructor call chain runs from derived to base, releasing derived resources first. The chapter provides a concrete FileLogger example where the derived class allocates a buffer; with a non-virtual base destructor the buffer leaks. In practice, always mark the destructor virtual in polymorphic base classes, even if the body is defaulted. When combined with smart pointers like unique_ptr, virtual destructors ensure predictable destruction order. A common misconception is that virtual destructors are only for rare cases — in polymorphic hierarchies they are essential. If the base class is intended purely as an interface with no state, prefer virtual defaulted destructors to guarantee safety without additional code. The final question to hold in mind: what could happen in a long-running system if cleanup is skipped?

Pure virtual functions are the language tool for expressing an abstract operation without providing a base implementation. You write a pure virtual function by appending equals zero to its declaration, for example declare virtual void draw() const = 0; in a Drawable base. Any class with one or more pure virtual functions becomes abstract and cannot be instantiated. Its purpose is to define a contract: derived classes must implement the pure virtual functions or themselves remain abstract. This pattern is the closest C++ has to an interface: a class with only pure virtual functions and a virtual destructor effectively defines a behavior contract that all implementers must follow. Concrete benefit: the compiler enforces that derived types implement required methods, preventing omissions at runtime. A misconception is that pure virtual functions must never have an implementation; in fact you can provide a base implementation while still making the function pure virtual, but that's an advanced use for shared functionality. The typical use is to keep the base lean and force derived types to supply the behavior. When designing systems, use abstract classes to capture the responsibilities you expect every implementer to have, then write code that depends only on that contract.
